title: Ezekiel 16:15–22
context: The LORD now charges Jerusalem with unfaithfulness. Trusting in her beauty and fame, she turned the gifts he gave her, clothing, jewels, oil, incense, and food, into offerings for idols. The allegory uses the language of marital unfaithfulness for idolatry and alliances with other gods. Worst of all, she sacrificed her children, whom the LORD calls “my children,” by making them pass through the fire, a practice Scripture condemns elsewhere (Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 16:3; 21:6; Jeremiah 7:31). Through it all she did not remember the days of her youth. These notes treat the allegory's language soberly and focus on its meaning for Jerusalem.

verses.text: “ ‘ “But you trusted in your beauty, and played the prostitute because of your renown, and poured out your prostitution on everyone who passed by. It was his.
verses.arminianNotes: “But you trusted in your beauty.” Arminian readers see the turning point: Jerusalem relied on the gift instead of the Giver and turned her renown into unfaithfulness, a real and culpable choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that trust misplaced in received gifts is the root of the sin described. The allegory uses marital language for idolatry, which both traditions read as the main point rather than the imagery itself.

verses.text: You took some of your garments, and made for yourselves high places decked with various colors, and played the prostitute on them. This shouldn’t happen, neither shall it be.
verses.arminianNotes: “You took some of your garments, and made for yourselves high places.” Arminian readers see the LORD's gifts used to decorate places of idol worship, turning blessing into betrayal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the high places, centers of worship outside the LORD's appointed way that the historical books often condemn. The phrase “This shouldn’t happen, neither shall it be” expresses the LORD's verdict.

verses.text: You also took your beautiful jewels of my gold and of my silver, which I had given you, and made for yourself images of men, and played the prostitute with them.
verses.arminianNotes: “You also took your beautiful jewels of my gold and of my silver.” Arminian readers see the stress on “my”: the LORD's own gifts were melted down to make idols, which deepens the offense.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that idolatry here involves turning God's gifts into objects of worship. Both traditions see a warning that blessings can be misused when the heart turns from the Giver.

verses.text: You took your embroidered garments, covered them, and set my oil and my incense before them.
verses.arminianNotes: “You took your embroidered garments, covered them.” Arminian readers see the LORD's fine clothing draped over idols, with “my oil and my incense” set before them as worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repeated “my” again. What belonged to the LORD's worship was offered to rivals, a reversal of the covenant relationship described in verses 8–14.

verses.text: My bread also which I gave you, fine flour, oil, and honey, with which I fed you, you even set it before them for a pleasant aroma; and so it was,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: “My bread also which I gave you.” Arminian readers see even the food of verse 13, “fine flour, oil, and honey,” offered to idols “for a pleasant aroma.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase “pleasant aroma” is usually used of offerings to the LORD. Here it is given to idols, which shows how worship itself was redirected.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Moreover you have taken your sons and your daughters, whom you have borne to me, and you have sacrificed these to them to be devoured. Was your prostitution a small matter,
verses.arminianNotes: “Moreover you have taken your sons and your daughters, whom you have borne to me.” Arminian readers see the gravest charge: children belonging to the LORD were sacrificed to idols.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the LORD’s rhetorical rebuke that this was no small matter. Child sacrifice is the climax of the indictment, and both traditions read it with sober horror.

verses.text: that you have slain my children and delivered them up, in causing them to pass through the fire to them?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD claims the children as his own. Arminian readers see that claim making their sacrifice a direct offense against him. Leviticus 18:21 had forbidden giving children “as a sacrifice to Molech.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare 2 Kings 16:3 and 21:6, which report kings of Judah who made a son “pass through the fire.” These notes name the parallels without assigning the verse to one event.

verses.text: In all your abominations and your prostitution you have not remembered the days of your youth, when you were naked and bare, and were wallowing in your blood.
verses.arminianNotes: “you have not remembered the days of your youth.” Arminian readers see forgetfulness of grace as the root of the sin: Jerusalem forgot she had once been helpless and rescued.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the refrain of remembering, which returns at verses 43 and 60–63. Forgetting the LORD's mercy leads to unfaithfulness, and remembering it is part of restoration.
